headline: Sea Bright Rocks at First Light: Blues on the Bunker, Bass Gone to Ground
subhead: The bluefish blitz we flagged last week finally rolled north into Sea Bright — the stripers, meanwhile, want nothing to do with daylight.
body_markdown:
Five-forty a.m., low tide plus an hour at the Sea Bright rocks, and I'm standing next to a kid I've never met who's got a Super Strike Zig Zag tied on and no idea what he's about to see. A bunker pod the size of a tennis court comes boiling down the beach, and it erupts — blues, blues, blues, tails slapping white water into the gray light. He hooks up on his third cast. So do I, on a chartreuse Danny swimmer worked half-speed across the seam off the third jetty down from the lighthouse. Ten-, eleven-pound blues, mean as hell, cutting leaders if you let them get bulldog on you. This is the bunker blitz we said last week would push north out of Raritan Bay and show itself along this stretch within a couple days — and here it is, right on schedule, right on the rocks at Sea Bright.

That's the daytime story right now, and it's a good one if you don't mind losing a few plugs to bluefish teeth. The blitz windows have been running on both the last hour of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming — bait gets pinned against the jetty faces at Sea Bright and up through Monmouth Beach, and the blues come through in waves, not a steady grind but real windows, twenty, thirty minutes of chaos and then quiet for an hour. Bring wire or heavy fluoro if you want to keep your plug inventory intact. Poppers on top when they're up, bucktails with a stinger hook worked through the wash when they've sounded.

Stripers are a different animal entirely this week, and if you're only fishing daylight hours you're going to think they left the building. They haven't — they've gone nocturnal, plain and simple. Surface temps sitting in the low-to-mid 70s off the beach have pushed the bass down onto structure and current seams during the day, and they're not interested in showing themselves again until the sun's well down and the water cools a degree or two. I worked the Manasquan Inlet jetties three nights running this week — the north side rocks on the last two hours of the incoming, fishing whole bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig in about 15 feet of water tight to the rock pile. Two keepers Tuesday night, one Thursday, nothing spectacular but real fish, 28 to 33 inches, and every one of them came after 10 p.m. Eels are doing work too — a rigged green eel drifted slow along the Shark River Inlet south jetty on the dropping tide picked up a fish just short of 30 inches for a guy I know from Belmar who's fished that same fifteen feet of rock for longer than I've been walking this beach.

Fluke have softened up in the shallow stuff, same story as everywhere else on this coast right now — the flats have gone quiet and the fish have slid into the deeper, moving water where it stays cooler. Manasquan Inlet channel, particularly the bend just inside the rock jetties where the current squeezes through, has been the most consistent producer. I've been dragging a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet right along the bottom on the last of the outgoing, and it's been good for a fish or two a drift — nothing over 20 inches, mostly 16 to 18, so you're culling through shorts to find keepers, but they're there. Shark River Inlet is fishing the same way — work the deeper edge on the channel side of the railroad bridge, outgoing water, and don't be afraid to slow the drift down with a little extra lead. The fish holding there right now aren't chasing anything fast.

Porgies have been a reliable, unglamorous bite around the Manasquan Inlet rock piles and the Spring Lake jetties — sandworms or clam on a high-low rig, bottom in 10 to 15 feet, any stage of tide really, though I like it best on the last two hours of the incoming when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Good for a bucket of dinner fish if the blitz and the bass game leave you wanting a slower afternoon. Blackfish season's closed up here through the summer, so that's a fall conversation — I'll get back to the tautog talk once October rolls around.

Wind's been the wildcard the last few days, and it's worth watching — a stiff onshore breeze can shut down the rock fishing at Sea Bright fast by chopping up the water and pushing the bait off the beach entirely, so if you see white water building and no bunker showing, don't waste your morning, go straight to the inlets instead. The moon's waxing toward full in early August, which means building current through both Manasquan and Shark River inlets over the next week — that should sharpen up the fluke bite in the channels and probably tighten the window on the nighttime bass bite too, concentrating them harder on the current seams instead of spread out over open structure.

My read for the coming week: the blitz should keep working its way along this stretch as long as the bunker keep moving north, so I'd be at Sea Bright or Monmouth Beach at first light watching for birds and nervous water before you do anything else. For bass, forget the sunrise patrol — set your alarm for 9 or 10 p.m. instead and fish the inlet jetties on bunker chunks or eels through the incoming. And for fluke, the deeper inlet bends are outproducing the open flats right now, so that's where I'd put my drift time if I only had one tide to fish.
